faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such an orientation that, as seen from Earth, one star periodically passes in front of the other. During these eclipses, the total brightness of the system dips. By measuring the depth, duration, and timing of these dips in a light curve, astronomers can infer the sizes, brightnesses, and orbital properties of the two stars.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is any star that passed our statistical tests and novelty check (it was not already listed in six known variable-star catalogs). A 'confirmed' candidate is one that also passed our automated pixel-level check, which confirms the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself and not from a nearby star that contaminated the measurement. Being confirmed means it passed our pipeline; it does not mean it has been independently verified or studied by other researchers.
faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean on this site, and how is it different from 'confirmed'?

faqs.answer: We trained a machine-learning model on 2007 labeled examples to provide a second opinion on candidate quality. It outperforms our rule-based baseline. However, the ML score is informational only - it does not currently filter or gate which candidates get checked. All candidates that pass our statistical and novelty checks proceed to the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score listed for some candidates?

faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated process that examines whether the eclipse signal is concentrated on the target star's location in the image or spread across nearby pixels. If the signal is centered on-target, the candidate passes. This check confirms that the eclipsing binary is genuinely at the position we thought, not a false alarm caused by a nearby star.
faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?

faqs.answer: Sometimes a light curve can be ambiguous about the true orbital period if eclipses are very shallow or noisy. The period-alias check compares the depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If they differ significantly, it may indicate we are seeing an alias - half the true period - rather than the real one. Any candidate flagged for this issue will carry a note on its individual page.
faqs.question: What is the period-alias check, and why might a candidate need it?

faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate links to its TESS light curve data, which is publicly available. You can download the data and inspect the eclipse pattern yourself. You can also cross-check the candidate against the six catalogs we use (VSX, ASAS-SN, Gaia eclipsing-binary table, Gaia variable classification, TESS EB catalog, and ExoFOP TOI list) to confirm it was not already known.
faqs.question: Can I verify a confirmed candidate myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the endpoint of this pipeline itself. We do not conduct follow-up observations, perform spectroscopy, measure stellar masses, or submit candidates for publication. That work would be up to other researchers who find value in our list. Some candidates may carry caveats or open questions noted on their individual pages; these are listed so you have the full picture before deciding whether a candidate interests you.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. Eclipsing binaries are pairs of stars that orbit each other and periodically block each other's light as seen from Earth, creating a distinctive pattern in brightness over time. Our pipeline samples target stars from TESS observations, applies statistical tests to separate real eclipsing binaries from noise and artifacts, cross-checks against six known variable-star catalogs to avoid re-listing known objects, and then runs an automated pixel-level check on each candidate to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby neighbor. We've confirmed 195 candidates so far, representing about 1.6% of the sky area we've sampled. Each candidate is listed here with its measured orbital period and eclipse depths. The process prioritizes precision: we filter aggressively to keep false positives low, and we note any remaining caveats on individual candidate pages so users can assess what further work might be needed.
